1	# RadixExperiment
2	
3	Radix is a verified embedded DSL built entirely by 10 AI agents (all Claude) in a single weekend.
4	This repository contains the Radix source code and a [Verso](https://github.com/leanprover/verso)-based slide deck
5	presenting the results: **"Lean for AI, AI for Lean"**.
6	
7	## What Radix demonstrates
8	
9	- **Zero `sorry`** — 52 theorems, all complete
10	- 5 verified compiler optimizations (constant folding, dead code elimination, copy propagation, constant propagation, inlining)
11	- Big-step semantics (16 rules) with determinism proof
12	- Interpreter correctness — sound and complete w.r.t. relational semantics
13	- Linear ownership typing with soundness proof (644-line invariant preservation)
14	- 27 modules, ~7,400 lines of Lean
15	
16	Zero lines were written by a human. The agents had full autonomy.
17	
18	## Examples
19	
20	Radix programs are written using concrete syntax macros (`[RStmt|...]`) that Lean elaborates and type-checks:
21	
22	```lean
23	def factorial := `[RStmt|
24	  n := 12;
25	  result := 1;
26	  while (n > 0) {
27	    result := result * n;
28	    n := n - 1;
29	  }
30	]
31	
32	#eval! run factorial "result"
33	-- 479001600
34	```
35	
36	Heap-allocated arrays with manual memory management:
37	
38	```lean
39	def sumOfSquares := `[RStmt|
40	  let arr := new uint64[][10];
41	  i := 0;
42	  while (i < 10) {
43	    arr[i] := (i + 1) * (i + 1);
44	    i := i + 1;
45	  }
46	  sum := 0;
47	  i := 0;
48	  while (i < 10) {
49	    sum := sum + arr[i];
50	    i := i + 1;
51	  }
52	  free(arr);
53	]
54	
55	#eval! run sumOfSquares "sum"
56	-- 385
57	```

66	      retTy := .unit

8	/-! # Radix AST
9	
10	Core abstract syntax for the Radix DSL. The design follows a standard imperative
11	language structure: expressions are pure (no side effects, no function calls),
12	statements handle control flow and mutation, and programs bundle function
13	declarations with a main statement.
14	
15	Key design choices:
16	- Expressions do not include function calls; calls are statement-level only
17	  (`callStmt`), which simplifies the semantics considerably.
18	- `scope` is the internal representation of an inlined function call: it pushes
19	  a fresh frame, binds parameters, executes a body, then pops the frame.
20	  The `inline` optimization rewrites `callStmt` into `scope`.
21	- Values include `addr` for heap-allocated arrays, but `addr` is not a source-level
22	  type -- it only appears at runtime.
23	-/
24	
25	namespace Radix
26	
27	/-! ## Types -/
28	
29	/-- Radix type system. `fn` is included for potential future use but is not
30	currently checked by the type checker. `array` types are heap-allocated and
31	accessed via `addr` values at runtime. -/
32	inductive Ty where
33	  | uint64
34	  | bool
35	  | unit
36	  | string
37	  | array : Ty → Ty
38	  | fn : List Ty → Ty → Ty
39	  deriving Repr, Inhabited, BEq
40	
41	/-! ## Values -/
42	
43	/-- Heap address, used as a key into `Heap.store`. -/
44	abbrev Addr := Nat
45	
46	/-- Runtime values. `addr` is not a source-level construct -- it arises only
47	from `alloc` at runtime. The `str` constructor wraps Lean `String` directly,
48	so string operations use the host string implementation. -/
49	inductive Value where
50	  | uint64 : UInt64 → Value
51	  | bool : Bool → Value
52	  | unit : Value
53	  | str : String → Value
54	  | addr : Addr → Value
55	  deriving Repr, Inhabited, DecidableEq, BEq
56	
57	/-! ## Operators -/
58	
59	inductive BinOp where
60	  | add | sub | mul | div | mod
61	  | eq | ne | lt | le | gt | ge
62	  | and | or
63	  | strAppend
64	  deriving Repr, DecidableEq, Inhabited, BEq
65	
66	inductive UnaryOp where
67	  | not | neg
68	  deriving Repr, DecidableEq, Inhabited, BEq
69	
70	/-! ## Expressions -/
71	
72	/-- Expressions are pure: they read from the environment and heap but never
73	modify them. No function calls -- those are statement-level. -/
74	inductive Expr where
75	  | lit : Value → Expr
76	  | var : String → Expr
77	  | binop : BinOp → Expr → Expr → Expr
78	  | unop : UnaryOp → Expr → Expr
79	  | arrGet : Expr → Expr → Expr
80	  | arrLen : Expr → Expr
81	  | strLen : Expr → Expr
82	  | strGet : Expr → Expr → Expr
83	  deriving Repr, Inhabited
84	
85	/-! ## Statements -/
86	
87	/-- Statements perform effects: variable mutation, heap allocation/free,
88	control flow, and function calls. `scope` is the frame-isolated form used
89	by the inliner -- it pushes a fresh frame with bound parameters, runs the
90	body, then pops the frame. -/
91	inductive Stmt where
92	  | skip
93	  | assign : String → Expr → Stmt
94	  | seq : Stmt → Stmt → Stmt
95	  | ite : Expr → Stmt → Stmt → Stmt
96	  | while : Expr → Stmt → Stmt
97	  | decl : String → Ty → Expr → Stmt
98	  | alloc : String → Ty → Expr → Stmt
99	  | free : Expr → Stmt
100	  | arrSet : Expr → Expr → Expr → Stmt
101	  | ret : Expr → Stmt
102	  | block : List Stmt → Stmt
103	  | callStmt : String → List Expr → Stmt
104	  | scope : List (String × Ty) → List Expr → Stmt → Stmt
105	  deriving Repr, Inhabited
106	
107	infixr:130 " ;; " => Stmt.seq
108	
109	/-! ## Function Declarations and Programs -/
110	
111	/-- A function declaration. Functions are called via `Stmt.callStmt`, which
112	pushes a new frame, binds arguments, executes the body, then pops the frame. -/
113	structure FunDecl where
114	  name : String
115	  params : List (String × Ty)
116	  retTy : Ty
117	  body : Stmt
118	  deriving Repr, Inhabited

7	import Radix.Env
8	import Radix.Heap
9	
10	/-! # Radix Program State
11	
12	The runtime state combines a call stack (list of `Frame`s), a heap, and a
13	function table. The call stack grows on function calls (`pushFrame`) and
14	shrinks on return (`popFrame`). Variable lookup and mutation always operate
15	on the topmost frame -- there is no variable capture across frames.
16	-/
17	
18	namespace Radix
19	open Std
20	
21	/-- A single stack frame: a local variable environment and an optional return
22	variable name (currently unused but reserved for future call-with-result). -/
23	structure Frame where
24	  env : Env := Env.empty
25	  retVar : Option String := none
26	  deriving Inhabited
27	
28	/-- The complete program state. `frames` is a stack (head = current frame).
29	`funs` is immutable after initialization -- the `BigStep.funs_preserved`
30	theorem in `Radix.Opt.Inline` proves this invariant. -/
31	structure PState where
32	  frames : List Frame := [{}]
33	  heap : Heap := {}
34	  funs : HashMap String FunDecl := {}
35	  deriving Inhabited
36	
37	namespace PState
38	
39	def currentFrame (σ : PState) : Option Frame :=
40	  σ.frames.head?
41	
42	def updateCurrentFrame (σ : PState) (f : Frame → Frame) : Option PState :=
43	  match σ.frames with
44	  | [] => none
45	  | fr :: rest => some { σ with frames := f fr :: rest }
46	
47	def getVar (σ : PState) (x : String) : Option Value := do
48	  let fr ← σ.currentFrame
49	  fr.env.get? x
50	
51	def setVar (σ : PState) (x : String) (v : Value) : Option PState :=
52	  σ.updateCurrentFrame fun fr => { fr with env := fr.env.set x v }
53	
54	def pushFrame (σ : PState) (fr : Frame) : PState :=
55	  { σ with frames := fr :: σ.frames }
56	
57	def popFrame (σ : PState) : Option (Frame × PState) :=
58	  match σ.frames with
59	  | [] => none
60	  | fr :: rest => some (fr, { σ with frames := rest })
61	
62	def lookupFun (σ : PState) (name : String) : Option FunDecl :=
63	  σ.funs.get? name
64	
65	/-- Build the initial state from a program: empty frame, empty heap,
66	function table populated from the program's declarations. -/
67	def initFromProgram (p : Program) : PState :=
68	  let funs := p.funs.foldl (init := ({}:HashMap String FunDecl)) fun m fd => m.insert fd.name fd
69	  { frames := [{}], heap := {}, funs }
70	
71	end PState
72	end Radix
73

1	/-
2	Copyright (c) 2026 Lean FRO, LLC. All rights reserved.
3	Released under Apache 2.0 license as described in the file LICENSE.
4	Authors: Leonardo de Moura
5	-/
6	
7	import Radix.AST
8	import Std.Data.HashMap
9	
10	/-! # Radix Heap Model
11	
12	A simple bump-allocator heap mapping addresses to `Array Value`. Each `alloc`
13	returns a fresh address (monotonically increasing `nextAddr`). The heap does
14	not reuse freed addresses, which simplifies the memory safety proofs
15	(`no_use_after_free`, `no_double_free` in `Radix.Proofs.MemorySafety`).
16	
17	All heap operations (`read`, `write`, `free`) return `Option` to model failures
18	(invalid address, out-of-bounds index) explicitly.
19	-/
20	
21	namespace Radix
22	open Std
23	
24	/-- The heap: a map from addresses to arrays of values, plus a bump counter
25	for fresh address allocation. -/
26	structure Heap where
27	  store : HashMap Nat (Array Value) := {}
28	  nextAddr : Nat := 0
29	  deriving Inhabited
30	
31	namespace Heap
32	
33	def alloc (h : Heap) (vals : Array Value) : Addr × Heap :=
34	  let a := h.nextAddr
35	  (a, { store := h.store.insert a vals, nextAddr := a + 1 })
36	
37	def free (h : Heap) (a : Addr) : Option Heap :=
38	  if h.store.contains a then
39	    some { h with store := h.store.erase a }
40	  else
41	    none
42	
43	def lookup (h : Heap) (a : Addr) : Option (Array Value) :=
44	  h.store.get? a
45	
46	def read (h : Heap) (a : Addr) (i : Nat) : Option Value := do
47	  let arr ← h.lookup a
48	  arr[i]?
49	
50	def write (h : Heap) (a : Addr) (i : Nat) (v : Value) : Option Heap := do
51	  let arr ← h.lookup a
52	  if hi : i < arr.size then
53	    some { h with store := h.store.insert a (arr.set i v) }
54	  else
55	    none
56	
57	def arraySize (h : Heap) (a : Addr) : Option Nat := do
58	  let arr ← h.lookup a
59	  return arr.size
60	
61	end Heap
62	end Radix
63	
```

7	import Radix.AST
8	import Std.Data.HashMap
9	
10	/-! # Radix Variable Environment
11	
12	A thin wrapper around `HashMap String Value` for variable environments.
13	Each `Frame` contains one `Env`. Variable scoping is handled by the
14	frame stack in `PState`, not by nested environments -- there is no
15	lexical scoping or closure capture.
16	-/
17	
18	namespace Radix
19	open Std
20	
21	abbrev Env := HashMap String Value
22	
23	namespace Env
24	
25	def empty : Env := {}
26	
27	def get? (env : Env) (x : String) : Option Value :=
28	  HashMap.get? env x
29	
30	def set (env : Env) (x : String) (v : Value) : Env :=
31	  HashMap.insert env x v
32	
33	def remove (env : Env) (x : String) : Env :=
34	  HashMap.erase env x
35	
36	end Env
37	end Radix
38

53	/-! # Radix: A Verified Embedded Imperative DSL
54	
55	Radix is an imperative DSL embedded in Lean 4 with:
56	- **Types**: `uint64`, `bool`, `string`, `unit`, heap-allocated `array α`
57	- **Control flow**: `if/else`, `while`, `return`, function calls with frame isolation
58	- **Dynamic memory**: `alloc`, `free`, bounds-checked array access
59	- **Two semantics**: relational big-step (`BigStep`) and executable fuel-based (`Stmt.interp`)
60	- **Verified optimizations**: constant folding, dead code elimination, copy propagation,
61	  constant propagation, function inlining -- each with a mechanized proof that it
62	  preserves big-step semantics
63	- **Formal properties**: determinism, type preservation, memory safety (no use-after-free,
64	  no double-free), linear ownership typing with soundness proof
65	- **Concrete syntax**: `\`[RExpr| ...]` and `\`[RStmt| ...]` macros for natural notation
66	
67	The architecture follows a classic compiler pipeline: AST -> type check -> optimize -> interpret.
68	Each optimization is a function `Stmt -> Stmt` paired with a theorem
69	`BigStep sigma s r -> BigStep sigma (s.opt) r`, ensuring semantic preservation.

9	/-! # Radix Expression Evaluation
10	
11	Defines evaluation for binary operators, unary operators, and expressions.
12	All operations return `Option Value` -- `none` means a runtime error
13	(type mismatch, division by zero, out-of-bounds access, etc.).
14	
15	Expression evaluation is pure: it reads from the program state but never
16	modifies it. This separation is what makes the optimization correctness
17	proofs tractable -- expression-level rewrites only need to preserve
18	`Expr.eval`, not the full `BigStep` relation.
19	-/
20	
21	namespace Radix
22	
23	/-- Evaluate a binary operator. Returns `none` on type mismatch or division
24	by zero. Marked `@[simp]` so the optimization correctness proofs can
25	reduce concrete cases automatically. -/
26	@[simp] def BinOp.eval : BinOp → Value → Value → Option Value
27	  | .add, .uint64 a, .uint64 b => some (.uint64 (a + b))
28	  | .sub, .uint64 a, .uint64 b => some (.uint64 (a - b))
29	  | .mul, .uint64 a, .uint64 b => some (.uint64 (a * b))
30	  | .div, .uint64 a, .uint64 b => if b = 0 then none else some (.uint64 (a / b))
31	  | .mod, .uint64 a, .uint64 b => if b = 0 then none else some (.uint64 (a % b))
32	  | .eq,  a,         b         => some (.bool (a == b))
33	  | .ne,  a,         b         => some (.bool (a != b))
34	  | .lt,  .uint64 a, .uint64 b => some (.bool (a < b))
35	  | .le,  .uint64 a, .uint64 b => some (.bool (a ≤ b))
36	  | .gt,  .uint64 a, .uint64 b => some (.bool (a > b))
37	  | .ge,  .uint64 a, .uint64 b => some (.bool (a ≥ b))
38	  | .and, .bool a,   .bool b   => some (.bool (a && b))
39	  | .or,  .bool a,   .bool b   => some (.bool (a || b))
40	  | .strAppend, .str a, .str b => some (.str (a ++ b))
41	  | _, _, _ => none
42	
43	@[simp] def UnaryOp.eval : UnaryOp → Value → Option Value
44	  | .not, .bool b   => some (.bool !b)
45	  | .neg, .uint64 n => some (.uint64 (0 - n))
46	  | _, _ => none
47	
48	/-- Evaluate an expression in a program state. Function calls are not handled
49	here — they require the statement-level evaluator. -/
50	def Expr.eval (σ : PState) : Expr → Option Value
51	  | .lit v => some v
52	  | .var x => σ.getVar x
53	  | .binop op l r => do
54	    let vl ← l.eval σ
55	    let vr ← r.eval σ
56	    op.eval vl vr
57	  | .unop op e => do
58	    let v ← e.eval σ
59	    op.eval v
60	  | .arrGet arr idx => do
61	    let .addr a ← arr.eval σ | none
62	    let .uint64 i ← idx.eval σ | none
63	    σ.heap.read a i.toNat
64	  | .arrLen arr => do
65	    let .addr a ← arr.eval σ | none
66	    let sz ← σ.heap.arraySize a
67	    some (.uint64 sz.toUInt64)
68	  | .strLen s => do
69	    let .str sv ← s.eval σ | none
70	    some (.uint64 sv.length.toUInt64)
71	  | .strGet s idx => do
72	    let .str sv ← s.eval σ | none
73	    let .uint64 i ← idx.eval σ | none
74	    if i.toNat < sv.length then
75	      some (.str (String.Pos.Raw.get sv ⟨i.toNat⟩ |>.toString))
76	    else
77	      none
78	
79	
80	end Radix

9	/-! # Radix Big-Step Semantics
10	
11	Relational big-step semantics for statements, including function call/return.
12	
13	This is the reference semantics against which all optimizations are verified.
14	Each optimization proves: if `BigStep sigma s r`, then `BigStep sigma (s.opt) r`.
15	The `BigStep.det` theorem (`Radix.Proofs.Determinism`) shows that this relation
16	is deterministic, so the original and optimized programs are observationally
17	equivalent.
18	
19	The semantics uses `StmtResult` to distinguish normal completion from early
20	return. The `seqReturn` rule short-circuits: if the first statement in a
21	sequence returns, the second is never executed.
22	-/
23	
24	namespace Radix
25	
26	/-- Result of executing a statement: either normal completion or a return. -/
27	inductive StmtResult where
28	  | normal : PState → StmtResult
29	  | returned : Value → PState → StmtResult
30	
31	/-- Extract the state from a result. -/
32	def StmtResult.state : StmtResult → PState
33	  | .normal σ => σ
34	  | .returned _ σ => σ
35	
36	/-- Big-step operational semantics for Radix statements.
37	
38	Notation: `⟨sigma, s⟩ ⇓ r` means statement `s` in state `sigma` produces
39	result `r`. The relation is deterministic (`BigStep.det`) and total for
40	well-typed, terminating programs. -/
41	inductive BigStep : PState → Stmt → StmtResult → Prop where
42	  | skip :
43	    BigStep σ .skip (.normal σ)
44	
45	  | assign (he : e.eval σ = some v) (hs : σ.setVar x v = some σ') :
46	    BigStep σ (.assign x e) (.normal σ')
47	
48	  | decl (he : e.eval σ = some v) (hs : σ.setVar x v = some σ') :
49	    BigStep σ (.decl x _ty e) (.normal σ')
50	
51	  | seqNormal (h₁ : BigStep σ₁ s₁ (.normal σ₂)) (h₂ : BigStep σ₂ s₂ r) :
52	    BigStep σ₁ (s₁ ;; s₂) r
53	
54	  | seqReturn (h₁ : BigStep σ₁ s₁ (.returned v σ₂)) :
55	    BigStep σ₁ (s₁ ;; s₂) (.returned v σ₂)
56	
57	  | ifTrue (hc : e.eval σ = some (.bool true)) (ht : BigStep σ t r) :
58	    BigStep σ (.ite e t f) r
59	
60	  | ifFalse (hc : e.eval σ = some (.bool false)) (hf : BigStep σ f r) :

63	  | whileTrue (hc : e.eval σ₁ = some (.bool true))

9	/-! # Radix Fuel-Based Interpreter
10	
11	Executable interpreter using fuel to guarantee termination. This is the
12	"runnable" counterpart to the relational `BigStep` semantics -- useful for
13	testing and `#guard` assertions, and the subject of the interpreter
14	correctness proofs (`Radix.Proofs.InterpCorrectness`).
15	
16	The interpreter returns `Except String (Option Value) × PState`:
17	- `.ok none` means normal completion
18	- `.ok (some v)` means a `ret` was encountered with value `v`
19	- `.error msg` means a runtime error
20	-/
21	
22	namespace Radix
23	
24	def evalExpr (e : Expr) (σ : PState) : Except String Value :=
25	  match e.eval σ with
26	  | some v => .ok v
27	  | none => .error "failed to evaluate expression"
28	
29	def evalArgs (args : List Expr) (σ : PState) : Except String (List Value) :=
30	  args.mapM (fun e => evalExpr e σ)
31	
32	def mkFrame (params : List (String × Ty)) (args : List Value) : Except String Frame := do
33	  if params.length ≠ args.length then
34	    throw s!"arity mismatch: expected {params.length} args, got {args.length}"
35	  let env := (params.zip args).foldl (fun e (p, v) => e.set p.1 v) Env.empty
36	  return { env }
37	
38	/-- Result type for the interpreter: either success with optional return value
39	and final state, or an error message. -/
40	abbrev InterpResult := Except String (Option Value) × PState
41	
42	/-- Helper: thread a successful non-returning result into a continuation. -/
43	@[inline] def andThen (r : InterpResult) (k : PState → InterpResult) : InterpResult :=
44	  match r with
45	  | (.ok none, σ') => k σ'
46	  | (.ok (some v), σ') => (.ok (some v), σ')
47	  | (.error e, σ') => (.error e, σ')
48	
49	/-- Fuel-based interpreter. Returns `(.ok none, σ')` for normal completion,
50	`(.ok (some v), σ')` when a `ret` statement is reached, or `(.error msg, σ)` on error. -/
51	def Stmt.interp (fuel : Nat) (s : Stmt) (σ : PState) : InterpResult :=
52	  match fuel with
53	  | 0 => (.error "out of fuel", σ)
54	  | fuel + 1 =>
55	    match s with
56	    | .skip => (.ok none, σ)
57	
58	    | .assign x e =>
59	      match evalExpr e σ with
60	      | .error msg => (.error msg, σ)
61	      | .ok v =>
62	        match σ.setVar x v with
63	        | some σ' => (.ok none, σ')
64	        | none => (.error "assign: no active frame", σ)
65	
66	    | .decl x _ty e =>
67	      match evalExpr e σ with
68	      | .error msg => (.error msg, σ)
69	      | .ok v =>
70	        match σ.setVar x v with
71	        | some σ' => (.ok none, σ')
72	        | none => (.error "decl: no active frame", σ)
73	
74	    | .seq s₁ s₂ =>
75	      andThen (s₁.interp fuel σ) (s₂.interp fuel)
76	
77	    | .ite c t f =>
78	      match evalExpr c σ with
79	      | .error msg => (.error msg, σ)
80	      | .ok (.bool true) => t.interp fuel σ
81	      | .ok (.bool false) => f.interp fuel σ
82	      | _ => (.error "if: condition must be bool", σ)
83	
84	    | .while c b =>
85	      match evalExpr c σ with
86	      | .error msg => (.error msg, σ)
87	      | .ok (.bool true) =>

89	      | .ok (.bool false) => (.ok none, σ)
90	      | _ => (.error "while: condition must be bool", σ)

100	        | none => (.error "alloc: no active frame", σ)
101	      | _ => (.error "alloc: size must be uint64", σ)

103	    | .free e =>

10	/-! # Radix Type Checking
11	
12	Type inference for Radix expressions. Given a type environment `TyEnv`
13	(mapping variable names to types) and function signatures `FunSigs`,
14	`Expr.typeOf` infers the type of an expression or returns `none` if
15	the expression is ill-typed.
16	
17	This module defines the typing rules used by the type safety proofs in
18	`Radix.Proofs.TypeSafety`. Statement-level type checking is not
19	implemented -- the current focus is expression-level preservation.
20	-/
21	
22	namespace Radix
23	open Std
24	
25	/-- Type environment: maps variable names to their declared types. -/
26	abbrev TyEnv := HashMap String Ty
27	
28	/-- Function signature table: maps function names to (parameter types, return type). -/
29	abbrev FunSigs := HashMap String (List Ty × Ty)
30	
31	@[simp] def BinOp.typeOfResult : BinOp → Ty → Ty → Option Ty
32	  | .add, .uint64, .uint64 | .sub, .uint64, .uint64
33	  | .mul, .uint64, .uint64 | .div, .uint64, .uint64
34	  | .mod, .uint64, .uint64 => some .uint64
35	  | .eq, a, b | .ne, a, b => if a == b then some .bool else none
36	  | .lt, .uint64, .uint64 | .le, .uint64, .uint64
37	  | .gt, .uint64, .uint64 | .ge, .uint64, .uint64 => some .bool
38	  | .and, .bool, .bool | .or, .bool, .bool => some .bool
39	  | .strAppend, .string, .string => some .string
40	  | _, _, _ => none
41	
42	@[simp] def UnaryOp.typeOfResult : UnaryOp → Ty → Option Ty
43	  | .not, .bool => some .bool
44	  | .neg, .uint64 => some .uint64
45	  | _, _ => none
46	
47	/-- Infer the type of an expression. -/
48	def Expr.typeOf (Γ : TyEnv) (sigs : FunSigs) : Expr → Option Ty
49	  | .lit (.uint64 _) => some .uint64
50	  | .lit (.bool _) => some .bool
51	  | .lit .unit => some .unit
52	  | .lit (.str _) => some .string
53	  | .lit (.addr _) => none
54	  | .var x => Γ.get? x
55	  | .binop op l r => do
56	    let tl ← l.typeOf Γ sigs
57	    let tr ← r.typeOf Γ sigs
58	    op.typeOfResult tl tr
59	  | .unop op e => do
60	    let t ← e.typeOf Γ sigs
61	    op.typeOfResult t
62	  | .arrGet arr idx => do
63	    let .array elemTy ← arr.typeOf Γ sigs | none
64	    let .uint64 ← idx.typeOf Γ sigs | none
65	    some elemTy
66	  | .arrLen arr => do
67	    let .array _ ← arr.typeOf Γ sigs | none
68	    some .uint64
69	  | .strLen s => do
70	    let .string ← s.typeOf Γ sigs | none
71	    some .uint64
72	  | .strGet s idx => do
73	    let .string ← s.typeOf Γ sigs | none
74	    let .uint64 ← idx.typeOf Γ sigs | none
75	    some .string
76	
77	end Radix

9	/-! # Radix Concrete Syntax
10	
11	Custom syntax categories for writing Radix programs naturally.
12	
13	Two syntax quotations are provided:
14	- `` `[RExpr| ...] `` for expressions: arithmetic, comparisons, booleans,
15	  string append, array indexing (`arr[i]`), and variable references.
16	- `` `[RStmt| ...] `` for statements: assignment, `let` declarations,
17	  `let ... := new T[n]` allocation, `if/else`, `while`, `free(...)`,
18	  array write, function calls, and `return`.
19	
20	Array length and string operations use helper macros `arrLen(...)`,
21	`strLen(...)`, `strGet(...)` that produce `Expr` values directly.
22	-/
23	
24	namespace Radix
25	
26	/-! ## Expression syntax -/
27	
28	syntax "`[RExpr|" term "]" : term
29	
30	macro_rules
31	  | `(`[RExpr| true])      => `(Expr.lit (.bool true))
32	  | `(`[RExpr| false])     => `(Expr.lit (.bool false))
33	  | `(`[RExpr| ()])        => `(Expr.lit .unit)
34	  | `(`[RExpr| $n:num])    => `(Expr.lit (.uint64 $n))
35	  | `(`[RExpr| $s:str])    => `(Expr.lit (.str $s))
36	  | `(`[RExpr| $x:ident])  => `(Expr.var $(Lean.quote x.getId.toString))
37	  | `(`[RExpr| ($x)])      => `(`[RExpr| $x])
38	  | `(`[RExpr| $x + $y])   => `(Expr.binop .add `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
39	  | `(`[RExpr| $x - $y])   => `(Expr.binop .sub `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
40	  | `(`[RExpr| $x * $y])   => `(Expr.binop .mul `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
41	  | `(`[RExpr| $x / $y])   => `(Expr.binop .div `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
42	  | `(`[RExpr| $x % $y])   => `(Expr.binop .mod `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
43	  | `(`[RExpr| $x == $y])  => `(Expr.binop .eq `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
44	  | `(`[RExpr| $x != $y])  => `(Expr.binop .ne `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
45	  | `(`[RExpr| $x < $y])   => `(Expr.binop .lt `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
46	  | `(`[RExpr| $x <= $y])  => `(Expr.binop .le `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
47	  | `(`[RExpr| $x > $y])   => `(Expr.binop .gt `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
48	  | `(`[RExpr| $x >= $y])  => `(Expr.binop .ge `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
49	  | `(`[RExpr| $x && $y])  => `(Expr.binop .and `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
50	  | `(`[RExpr| $x || $y])  => `(Expr.binop .or `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
51	  | `(`[RExpr| $x ++ $y])  => `(Expr.binop .strAppend `[RExpr| $x] `[RExpr| $y])
52	  | `(`[RExpr| !$x])       => `(Expr.unop .not `[RExpr| $x])
53	  | `(`[RExpr| $a[$i]])    => `(Expr.arrGet `[RExpr| $a] `[RExpr| $i])
54	
55	/-! ## Helper macros for array/string expression forms -/
56	
57	scoped syntax:max "arrLen(" term ")" : term
58	scoped syntax:max "strLen(" term ")" : term
59	scoped syntax:max "strGet(" term "," term ")" : term
60	
61	scoped macro_rules

9	/-! # Determinism of Big-Step Semantics
10	
11	Proof that the big-step semantics is deterministic: if a statement evaluates
12	to two results from the same state, those results must be equal.
13	
14	This is a foundational property -- it means the optimization correctness
15	theorems (`constFold_correct`, `deadCodeElim_correct`, etc.) actually imply
16	observational equivalence, not just that the optimized program is one
17	possible behavior.
18	
19	The proof uses `grind` for cases that reduce to equational contradictions
20	or functional injectivity (e.g., `some true = some false` is absurd),
21	and explicit inductive hypothesis application for recursive cases
22	(`seq`, `while`, `call`).
23	-/
24	
25	namespace Radix
26	
27	/-- The big-step semantics is deterministic: same state + same statement
28	implies same result. -/
29	theorem BigStep.det (h₁ : BigStep σ s r₁) (h₂ : BigStep σ s r₂) : r₁ = r₂ := by
30	  induction h₁ generalizing r₂ with
31	  | skip => cases h₂; rfl
32	  | assign he₁ hs₁ => cases h₂ with | assign => grind
33	  | decl he₁ hs₁ => cases h₂ with | decl => grind
34	  | ifTrue hc₁ ht₁ iht => cases h₂ with
35	    | ifTrue _ ht₂ => exact iht ht₂
36	    | ifFalse hc₂ _ => grind
37	  | ifFalse hc₁ hf₁ ihf => cases h₂ with
38	    | ifTrue hc₂ _ => grind
39	    | ifFalse _ hf₂ => exact ihf hf₂
40	  | whileFalse hc₁ => cases h₂ with
41	    | whileTrue hc₂ _ _ => grind
42	    | whileReturn hc₂ _ => grind
43	    | whileFalse _ => rfl
44	  | alloc hsz₁ ha₁ hs₁ => cases h₂ with | alloc => grind
45	  | free he₁ hf₁ => cases h₂ with | free => grind
46	  | arrSet harr₁ hidx₁ hval₁ hw₁ => cases h₂ with | arrSet => grind
47	  | ret he₁ => cases h₂ with | ret => grind
48	  | block _ ihb => cases h₂ with | block hb₂ => exact ihb hb₂
49	  | seqNormal hs₁ hs₂ ih₁ ih₂ =>
50	    cases h₂ with
51	    | seqNormal hs₁' hs₂' => cases ih₁ hs₁'; exact ih₂ hs₂'
52	    | seqReturn hs₁' => cases ih₁ hs₁'
53	  | seqReturn hs₁ ih₁ =>
54	    cases h₂ with
55	    | seqNormal hs₁' _ => cases ih₁ hs₁'
56	    | seqReturn hs₁' => exact ih₁ hs₁'
57	  | whileTrue hc hb hw ihb ihw =>
58	    cases h₂ with
59	    | whileTrue _ hb₂ hw₂ => cases ihb hb₂; exact ihw hw₂
60	    | whileReturn _ hb₂ => cases ihb hb₂
61	    | whileFalse hc₂ => grind
62	  | whileReturn hc hb ihb =>
63	    cases h₂ with
64	    | whileTrue _ hb₂ _ => cases ihb hb₂
65	    | whileReturn _ hb₂ => exact ihb hb₂
66	    | whileFalse hc₂ => grind
67	  | callStmt hlook hargs hparams hframe hbody hpop ihbody =>
68	    cases h₂ with
69	    | callStmt hlook₂ hargs₂ hparams₂ hframe₂ hbody₂ hpop₂ =>
70	      simp_all [PState.lookupFun]
71	      cases ihbody hbody₂
72	      simp_all
73	  | scope hargs hlen hframe hbody hpop ihbody =>
74	    cases h₂ with
75	    | scope hargs₂ hlen₂ hframe₂ hbody₂ hpop₂ =>
76	      simp_all
77	      cases ihbody hbody₂
78	      simp_all
79	
80	end Radix

11	/-! # Type Safety
12	
13	Preservation theorem for the Radix type system.
14	
15	**Preservation** (`Expr.preservation`): if a well-typed expression evaluates
16	successfully, the result value has the expected type. The proof requires a
17	heap typing hypothesis (`hheapTy`) stating that heap contents match their
18	declared element types — standard in type safety proofs for languages with
19	mutable heap-allocated data.
20	
21	**Progress** is not included: "a well-typed expression always evaluates to
22	some value" is false for Radix because `e / 0`, out-of-bounds `arr[i]`, and
23	out-of-bounds `s[i]` are well-typed but evaluate to `none`. A correct
24	formulation would require a totality judgment or strengthened preconditions.
25	-/
26	
27	namespace Radix
28	open Std
29	
30	/-- A value is well-typed if it matches the expected type. -/
31	def Value.hasType : Value → Ty → Prop
32	  | .uint64 _, .uint64 => True
33	  | .bool _,   .bool   => True
34	  | .unit,     .unit    => True
35	  | .str _,    .string  => True
36	  | .addr _,   .array _ => True
37	  | _, _ => False
38	
39	/-- Literal values have the type assigned by `typeOf`. -/
40	private theorem lit_hasType (v : Value) (ty : Ty)
41	    (hty : Expr.typeOf Γ sigs (.lit v) = some ty) :
42	    Value.hasType v ty := by
43	  unfold Expr.typeOf at hty
44	  cases v <;> simp at hty <;> subst_vars <;> simp [Value.hasType]
45	
46	/-- Variables in a well-typed environment evaluate to well-typed values. -/
47	private theorem var_hasType (x : String) (ty : Ty) (v : Value) (σ : PState)
48	    (henv : ∀ x ty, Γ.get? x = some ty → ∃ v, σ.getVar x = some v ∧ Value.hasType v ty)
49	    (hty : Expr.typeOf Γ sigs (.var x) = some ty)
50	    (heval : Expr.eval σ (.var x) = some v) :
51	    Value.hasType v ty := by
52	  unfold Expr.typeOf at hty; unfold Expr.eval at heval
53	  have ⟨w, hw, hhas⟩ := henv x ty hty
54	  simp [hw] at heval; subst heval; exact hhas
55	
56	/-- Binary operation evaluation preserves types. -/
57	private theorem BinOp.eval_preserves_type {op : BinOp} {vl vr v : Value} {tl tr ty : Ty}
58	    (hvl : vl.hasType tl) (hvr : vr.hasType tr)
59	    (hty : op.typeOfResult tl tr = some ty)
60	    (hev : op.eval vl vr = some v) :
61	    v.hasType ty := by
62	  cases op
63	  all_goals (first
64	    | (-- eq and ne: eval works on any values, typeOfResult needs tl == tr
65	       simp [BinOp.eval] at hev; subst hev
66	       simp [BinOp.typeOfResult] at hty; obtain ⟨_, rfl⟩ := hty
67	       simp [Value.hasType])
68	    | (-- arithmetic without guards (add, sub, mul) and comparisons/logic
69	       cases tl <;> cases tr <;> simp [BinOp.typeOfResult] at hty
70	       subst hty
71	       cases vl <;> simp [Value.hasType] at hvl
72	       cases vr <;> simp [Value.hasType] at hvr
73	       simp [BinOp.eval] at hev; subst hev; simp [Value.hasType])
74	    | (-- div, mod: have an if guard
75	       cases tl <;> cases tr <;> simp [BinOp.typeOfResult] at hty
76	       subst hty
77	       cases vl <;> simp [Value.hasType] at hvl
78	       cases vr <;> simp [Value.hasType] at hvr
79	       simp [BinOp.eval] at hev; obtain ⟨_, rfl⟩ := hev; simp [Value.hasType]))
80	
81	/-- Unary operation evaluation preserves types. -/
82	private theorem UnaryOp.eval_preserves_type {op : UnaryOp} {v w : Value} {t ty : Ty}
83	    (hv : v.hasType t)
84	    (hty : op.typeOfResult t = some ty)
85	    (hev : op.eval v = some w) :
86	    w.hasType ty := by
87	  cases op <;> cases t <;> simp [UnaryOp.typeOfResult] at hty <;>
88	    subst ty <;> cases v <;> simp [Value.hasType] at hv <;>
89	    simp [UnaryOp.eval] at hev <;> subst hev <;> simp [Value.hasType]
90

1	/-

6	
7	import Radix.Heap
8	
9	/-! # Memory Safety Properties
10	
11	Proofs that the heap model enforces basic memory safety invariants:
12	- `no_use_after_free`: a freed address cannot be looked up
13	- `no_double_free`: a freed address cannot be freed again
14	- `read_within_bounds`: in-bounds reads on a live allocation always succeed
15	
16	These are properties of the `Heap` API, not of the full language -- they
17	show that the heap abstraction itself is sound. Full program-level memory
18	safety (e.g., "a well-typed program never performs use-after-free") would
19	require a linear type system or ownership tracking, which is future work.
20	-/
21	
22	namespace Radix
23	
24	/-- After freeing address `a`, looking it up returns `none`. -/
25	theorem Heap.no_use_after_free (h : Heap) (a : Addr) {h' : Heap}
26	    (hfree : h.free a = some h') : h'.lookup a = none := by
27	  unfold Heap.free at hfree
28	  split at hfree
29	  · simp at hfree
30	    unfold Heap.lookup
31	    rw [← hfree]
32	    simp
33	  · simp at hfree
34	
35	/-- After freeing address `a`, freeing it again returns `none`. -/
36	theorem Heap.no_double_free (h : Heap) (a : Addr) {h' : Heap}
37	    (hfree : h.free a = some h') : h'.free a = none := by
38	  unfold Heap.free at hfree
39	  split at hfree
40	  · simp at hfree
41	    unfold Heap.free
42	    rw [← hfree]
43	    simp [Std.HashMap.contains_erase]
44	  · simp at hfree
45	
46	/-- If `lookup` returns an array and `i` is within bounds, `read` succeeds. -/
47	theorem Heap.read_within_bounds (h : Heap) (a : Addr) (i : Nat) {arr : Array Value}
48	    (hlookup : h.lookup a = some arr) (hbounds : i < arr.size) :
49	    ∃ v, h.read a i = some v := by
50	  unfold Heap.read
51	  simp [hlookup, Array.getElem?_eq_getElem hbounds]
52	
53	end Radix
54

6	import Radix.Eval.Stmt

8	
9	/-! # Linear Ownership Typing for Memory Safety
10	
11	A linear ownership type system that tracks which variables hold live heap
12	addresses. `LinearOk O s O'` says statement `s` transforms owned-set `O`
13	to `O'`. Programs typed `∅ → ∅` are balanced (every alloc matched by free).
14	
15	The soundness theorem proves that the ownership invariant is preserved:
16	owned variables always point to live, distinct heap addresses.
17	-/
18	
19	namespace Radix
20	open Std
21	
22	abbrev Owned := HashSet String
23	
24	/-- Linear ownership typing judgment. `LinearOk O s O'` means statement `s`
25	transforms owned-set `O` to `O'`. -/
26	inductive LinearOk : Owned → Stmt → Owned → Prop where
27	  | skip : LinearOk O .skip O
28	  | assign (h : x ∉ O) : LinearOk O (.assign x e) O
29	  | decl (h : x ∉ O) : LinearOk O (.decl x ty e) O
30	  | seq (h1 : LinearOk O s1 O') (h2 : LinearOk O' s2 O'') :
31	      LinearOk O (s1 ;; s2) O''
32	  | ite (ht : LinearOk O t O') (hf : LinearOk O f O') :
33	      LinearOk O (.ite c t f) O'
34	  | whileLoop (hb : LinearOk O b O) :
35	      LinearOk O (.while c b) O
36	  | alloc (h : x ∉ O) :
37	      LinearOk O (.alloc x ty sz) (O.insert x)
38	  | free (h : x ∈ O) :
39	      LinearOk O (.free (.var x)) (O.erase x)
40	  | arrSet (h : x ∈ O) :
41	      LinearOk O (.arrSet (.var x) idx val) O
42	  | ret : LinearOk O (.ret e) O
43	  | block (h : LinearOk O (stmts.foldl (· ;; ·) .skip) O') :
44	      LinearOk O (.block stmts) O'
45	  | callStmt : LinearOk O (.callStmt name args) O
46	  | scope (h : LinearOk ∅ body ∅) :
47	      LinearOk O (.scope params args body) O
48	
49	/-- The ownership invariant: owned variables hold live, distinct heap addresses,
50	and the heap is well-formed (all stored addresses < nextAddr). -/
51	def OwnershipInv (σ : PState) (O : Owned) : Prop :=
52	  (∀ a, σ.heap.store.contains a → a < σ.heap.nextAddr) ∧
53	  (∀ x, x ∈ O →
54	    ∃ a, σ.getVar x = some (.addr a) ∧ σ.heap.lookup a ≠ none) ∧
55	  (∀ x y, x ∈ O → y ∈ O → x ≠ y →
56	    ∀ a b, σ.getVar x = some (.addr a) → σ.getVar y = some (.addr b) → a ≠ b)
57	
58	/-- All functions in the function table have linearly balanced bodies. -/
59	def WellTypedFuns (funs : HashMap String FunDecl) : Prop :=
60	  ∀ name fd, funs.get? name = some fd → LinearOk ∅ fd.body ∅

=== Radix/Opt/ConstFold.lean ===

import Radix.Eval.Stmt

/-! # Constant Folding

Fold constant expressions: `3 + 4 → 7`, `true && e → e`, etc.
Includes algebraic identity simplifications (e.g. `e + 0 → e`) guarded
by structural type inference, with a correctness proof that the
optimization preserves semantics.

## Identity vs. absorb rules

Identity simplifications like `e + 0 → e` are sound with a type guard: when
we know `e` produces a `uint64` (if it succeeds at all), then
`BinOp.eval .add v (.uint64 0) = some v`.

Absorb simplifications like `e * 0 → 0` are NOT sound without guaranteeing
that `e.eval σ` succeeds: if `e.eval σ = none`, the original expression
produces `none` but the simplified one produces `some (.uint64 0)`.  Since
`Expr.inferTag` cannot guarantee evaluation success (only the result type
when it does succeed), absorb rules are omitted.  They require a full type
system with totality guarantees to be sound.

namespace Radix

/-! ## Value type tags and structural type inference -/

/-- Type tag of a runtime value. -/
inductive ValTag where
  | uint64 | bool | str | unit | addr
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr

/-- Extract the type tag from a value. -/
@[simp] def Value.tag : Value → ValTag
  | .uint64 _ => .uint64
  | .bool _   => .bool
  | .str _    => .str
  | .unit     => .unit
  | .addr _   => .addr

/-- What tag does a `BinOp` produce when fed operands of the given tags? -/
@[simp] def BinOp.resultTag : BinOp → ValTag → ValTag → Option ValTag
  | .add, .uint64, .uint64 | .sub, .uint64, .uint64
  | .mul, .uint64, .uint64 | .div, .uint64, .uint64
  | .mod, .uint64, .uint64 => some .uint64
  | .eq, _, _ | .ne, _, _ => some .bool
  | .lt, .uint64, .uint64 | .le, .uint64, .uint64
  | .gt, .uint64, .uint64 | .ge, .uint64, .uint64 => some .bool
  | .and, .bool, .bool | .or, .bool, .bool => some .bool
  | .strAppend, .str, .str => some .str
  | _, _, _ => none

/-- What tag does a `UnaryOp` produce when fed an operand of the given tag? -/
@[simp] def UnaryOp.resultTag : UnaryOp → ValTag → Option ValTag

import Radix.Opt.ConstFold
import Std.Data.HashMap

/-! # Constant Propagation

Track which variables hold known constant values and substitute them.
Unlike constant folding (which only simplifies literal subexpressions),
constant propagation tracks the flow of constants through assignments:
`x := 5; y := x + 1` becomes `x := 5; y := 6` after propagation + folding.

The `ConstMap` records which variables are known to hold specific values.
Like copy propagation, the map is reset at control flow joins. After
substitution, constant folding is applied to maximize simplification.

The correctness proof follows the same pattern as copy propagation:
maintain a `ConstMap.agrees` invariant and show it holds after each
statement form.

namespace Radix
open Std

abbrev ConstMap := HashMap String Value

/-- Substitute known constants in an expression. -/
def Expr.constProp (m : ConstMap) : Expr → Expr
  | .lit v => .lit v
  | .var x => match m.get? x with
    | some v => .lit v
    | none => .var x
  | .binop op l r => .binop op (l.constProp m) (r.constProp m)
  | .unop op e => .unop op (e.constProp m)

import VersoSlides
import Slides

open VersoSlides

def main (args : List String) : IO UInt32 := do
  let config : Config := { center := false, margin := 0 }
  let rc ← slidesMain (config := config) (doc := %doc Slides) (args := args)
  let outputDir := config.outputDir
  -- Copy static assets into output directory
  let cssContents ← IO.FS.readFile "static/custom.css"
  IO.FS.writeFile (outputDir / "custom.css") cssContents
  let logoBytes ← IO.FS.readBinFile "static/lean-logo.png"
  IO.FS.writeBinFile (outputDir / "lean-logo.png") logoBytes
  -- Post-process HTML
  let htmlPath := outputDir / "index.html"
  let html ← IO.FS.readFile htmlPath
  -- Inject custom stylesheet at end of <head>
  let html := html.replace "</head>" "<link rel=\"stylesheet\" href=\"custom.css\">\n    </head>"
  -- Inject disableLayout into Reveal.initialize (the Stanford trick)
  let html := html.replace "Reveal.initialize({" "Reveal.initialize({\n        disableLayout: true,"
  -- Inject slide header (logo + line) into content slides (not dark slides)
  let slideHeader := "<div class=\"slide-header\"><img src=\"lean-logo.png\" alt=\"Lean\"></div>"
  -- Add header after each <section> that doesn't have data-background-color
  let html := html.replace "<section>\n" s!"<section>\n          {slideHeader}\n"
  let html := html.replace "<section data-transition=\"fade\">\n" s!"<section data-transition=\"fade\">\n          {slideHeader}\n"
  IO.FS.writeFile htmlPath html
  -- Inline hover data to avoid fetch CORS issues when opening as local files
  let docsJsonPath := outputDir / "-verso-docs.json"
  if ← docsJsonPath.pathExists then
    let docsJson ← IO.FS.readFile docsJsonPath
    -- Patch highlighting.js
    let hlJsPath := outputDir / "lib" / "highlighting.js"
    if ← hlJsPath.pathExists then
      let hlJs ← IO.FS.readFile hlJsPath
      let hlJs := hlJs.replace
        "fetch(docsJson).then((resp) => resp.json()).then((versoDocData) => {"
        s!"Promise.resolve({docsJson}).then((versoDocData) => \{"
      let hlJs := hlJs.replace
        "window.onload = () => {"
        "window.addEventListener('load', () => {"
      IO.FS.writeFile hlJsPath hlJs
    -- Patch panel.js
    let panelJsPath := outputDir / "lib" / "panel.js"
    if ← panelJsPath.pathExists then
      let panelJs ← IO.FS.readFile panelJsPath
      let panelJs := panelJs.replace
        "fetch(\"-verso-docs.json\")\n            .then(function (r) {\n                return r.ok ? r.json() : {};\n            })\n            .then(function (j) {\n                docsJson = j;\n            })\n            .catch(function () {\n                docsJson = {};\n            });"
        s!"docsJson = {docsJson};"
      IO.FS.writeFile panelJsPath panelJs
  return rc

import Radix.Syntax

/-! # Radix Examples

Executable programs demonstrating the DSL syntax and fuel-based interpreter.
Each example uses `#eval!` to run the program and display the result.

namespace Radix

/-- Display a Radix value in readable format. -/
def Value.display : Value → String
  | .uint64 n => toString n
  | .bool b   => toString b
  | .unit     => "()"
  | .str s    => s!"\"{s}\""
  | .addr a   => s!"<addr {a}>"

end Radix

namespace Radix.Examples

/-- Run a statement and display the value of variable `x`. -/
private def run (s : Stmt) (x : String) : String :=
  match s.run with
  | .ok σ => match σ.getVar x with
    | some v => v.display
    | none => s!"variable '{x}' not found"
  | .error msg => s!"error: {msg}"

/-- Inline small function calls in a statement.
    The `depth` parameter bounds the inlining depth, ensuring termination:
    `depth` decreases in the `callStmt` case (where we recurse on the inlined body),
    and the statement decreases structurally in all other cases. -/
def Stmt.inline (funs : HashMap String FunDecl) (depth : Nat) : Stmt → Stmt
  | .skip => .skip
  | .assign x e => .assign x e
  | .seq s₁ s₂ => .seq (s₁.inline funs depth) (s₂.inline funs depth)
  | .ite c t f => .ite c (t.inline funs depth) (f.inline funs depth)
  | .while c b => .while c (b.inline funs depth)
  | .decl x ty e => .decl x ty e
  | .alloc x ty sz => .alloc x ty sz
  | .free e => .free e
  | .arrSet a i v => .arrSet a i v
  | .ret e => .ret e
  | .block stmts => .block (Stmt.inlineList funs depth stmts)
  | .callStmt name args =>
    match depth with
    | 0 => .callStmt name args
    | depth' + 1 =>
      match funs.get? name with
      | some fd =>
        if fd.body.size ≤ inlineThreshold && !fd.body.containsCall name then
          .scope fd.params args (fd.body.inline funs depth')
        else
          .callStmt name args
      | none => .callStmt name args
  | .scope ps as body => .scope ps as (body.inline funs depth)

def Stmt.inlineList (funs : HashMap String FunDecl) (depth : Nat) : List Stmt → List Stmt

mutual
/-- Dead code elimination pass. -/
def Stmt.deadCodeElim : Stmt → Stmt
  | .skip => .skip
  | .assign x e => .assign x e
  | .seq s₁ s₂ =>
    match s₁.deadCodeElim with
    | .skip => s₂.deadCodeElim
    | s₁' =>
      match s₂.deadCodeElim with
      | .skip => s₁'
      | s₂' => .seq s₁' s₂'
  | .ite c t f =>
    match c with
    | .lit (.bool true) => t.deadCodeElim
    | .lit (.bool false) => f.deadCodeElim
    | _ =>
      match t.deadCodeElim, f.deadCodeElim with
      | .skip, .skip => .skip
      | t', f' => .ite c t' f'
  | .while c b =>
    match c with
    | .lit (.bool false) => .skip
    | _ => .while c b.deadCodeElim
  | .decl x ty e => .decl x ty e
  | .alloc x ty sz => .alloc x ty sz
  | .free e => .free e
  | .arrSet a i v => .arrSet a i v
  | .ret e => .ret e
  | .block stmts => .block (Stmt.deadCodeElimList stmts)
  | .callStmt f args => .callStmt f args
  | .scope ps as body => .scope ps as body.deadCodeElim

def Stmt.deadCodeElimList : List Stmt → List Stmt
  | [] => []
  | s :: ss => s.deadCodeElim :: Stmt.deadCodeElimList ss
end

private theorem BigStep.skip_eq (h : BigStep σ .skip r) : r = .normal σ := by
  cases h; rfl

private theorem dce_seq_to_seq_dce (h : BigStep σ (Stmt.deadCodeElim (a ;; b)) r) :
    BigStep σ (a.deadCodeElim ;; b.deadCodeElim) r := by
  simp only [Stmt.deadCodeElim] at h
  split at h
  next heq =>
    rw [heq]; exact BigStep.seqNormal BigStep.skip h
  next =>
    split at h
    next _ heq =>
      rw [heq]
      cases r with
      | normal σ' => exact BigStep.seqNormal h BigStep.skip
      | returned v σ' => exact BigStep.seqReturn h
    next => exact h

private theorem BigStep.foldl_seq_mono (xs : List Stmt)
    (hab : ∀ σ r, BigStep σ a r → BigStep σ b r)
    (h : BigStep σ (xs.foldl (init := a) (· ;; ·)) r) :
    BigStep σ (xs.foldl (init := b) (· ;; ·)) r := by
  induction xs generalizing a b σ r with
  | nil => simp [List.foldl] at *; exact hab σ r h
  | cons x xs ih =>
    simp only [List.foldl] at *
    apply ih (a := a ;; x) (b := b ;; x)
    · intro σ' r' h'
      cases h' with
      | seqNormal h₁ h₂ => exact BigStep.seqNormal (hab σ' _ h₁) h₂
      | seqReturn h₁ => exact BigStep.seqReturn (hab σ' _ h₁)
    · exact h

private theorem dce_foldl_gen (acc : Stmt) (stmts : List Stmt) (σ : PState) (r : StmtResult)
    (h : BigStep σ (Stmt.deadCodeElim (stmts.foldl (init := acc) (· ;; ·))) r) :
    BigStep σ ((Stmt.deadCodeElimList stmts).foldl (init := acc.deadCodeElim) (· ;; ·)) r := by
  induction stmts generalizing acc σ r with
  | nil => simp [Stmt.deadCodeElimList, List.foldl] at *; exact h
  | cons s ss ih =>
    simp only [List.foldl, Stmt.deadCodeElimList]
    have h' := ih (acc ;; s) σ r h
    exact BigStep.foldl_seq_mono (Stmt.deadCodeElimList ss)
      (fun σ r h => dce_seq_to_seq_dce h) h'

private theorem dce_foldl_skip (stmts : List Stmt) (σ : PState) (r : StmtResult)
    (h : BigStep σ (Stmt.deadCodeElim (stmts.foldl (init := Stmt.skip) (· ;; ·))) r) :
    BigStep σ ((Stmt.deadCodeElimList stmts).foldl (init := Stmt.skip) (· ;; ·)) r := by
  have := dce_foldl_gen Stmt.skip stmts σ r h
  simp [Stmt.deadCodeElim] at this; exact this

/-- Dead code elimination preserves big-step semantics. -/
theorem Stmt.deadCodeElim_correct (h : BigStep σ s r) : BigStep σ s.deadCodeElim r := by

Done. I explored `third-party/RadixExperiment/` and wrote the analysis to **`docs/RADIX-DESIGN.md`**, with an index line added to `docs/README.md`.

What the project is: **Radix**, a verified imperative DSL embedded in Lean 4 (~6.5k lines, 52 theorems, zero `sorry`), built per its README by 10 Claude agents in a weekend, packaged with a Verso slide deck ("Lean for AI, AI for Lean"). The checkout's git history is the slides repo (Leonardo de Moura / Lean FRO commits); the Radix sources were copied in from elsewhere.

The design choices the doc records, briefly:

- **Proof-shaped language design.** Every feature is bent toward provability: expressions are pure with no calls (so optimizations only preserve a first-order `Expr.eval` equation), the heap is a bump allocator that never reuses addresses (making `no_use_after_free`/`no_double_free` one-lemma facts), and the inliner rewrites calls into a `scope` construct **without substituting arguments** — semantically identical to a call minus the table lookup, so `inline_correct` is nearly a rule swap.
- **Two connected semantics.** Relational `BigStep` (16 rules) as reference, fuel-based executable interpreter, with soundness + completeness + fuel-monotonicity bridging them, and a determinism theorem that upgrades the per-pass results to observational equivalence.
- **Soundness-first optimizations.** When a rewrite would need an analysis they didn't have, they dropped the rewrite, not the theorem: absorb rules (`e*0→0`) refused as unsound under `Option`-partiality, dataflow maps reset to empty at control-flow joins instead of intersected, dead-*store* elimination built up to (`readVars`) but never used.
- **Two disconnected type layers.** Expression-level preservation only — progress is explicitly rejected with documented counterexamples — plus an opt-in linear ownership judgment `LinearOk O s O'` whose 643-line soundness proof uses a strengthened three-part induction (invariant / heap-wf / frame property) with balanced-callee obligations (`∅ → ∅`) for modular calls.
- **Everything is elaborator-checked.** Tests are 143 `#guard`s (build success = tests pass), slide code blocks elaborate against the real library, and the deck build post-processes reveal.js HTML to work offline.

The doc closes with takeaways that connect to this repo's own work (the two-semantics pattern, strengthened-conjunction induction, and the balanced-callee trick vs. LowIR's cross-call disjointness).

5	Verus is a tool for verifying the correctness of code written in Rust.
6	Developers write specifications of what their code should do,
7	and Verus statically checks that the executable Rust code will always 
8	satisfy the specifications for all possible executions of the code.
9	Rather than adding run-time checks, Verus instead relies on powerful solvers to
10	prove the code is correct.  Verus currently supports a subset of Rust (which we
11	are working to expand), and in some cases, it allows developers to go beyond
12	the standard Rust type system and statically check the correctness of code
13	that, for example, manipulates raw pointers.

2	
3	This document provides an overview of Verus internals for developers
4	contributing to the project. For build instructions and testing, see
5	[CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md).
6	
7	## Verification Pipeline Overview
8	
9	Verus transforms Rust source code through multiple intermediate representations:
10	
11	```
12	Rust Source Code
13	    ↓ (rustc: parsing, macro expansion)
14	Rust HIR (High-level Intermediate Representation)
15	    ↓ (rust_verify: HIR → VIR)
16	VIR-AST (Verification Intermediate Representation)
17	    ↓ (vir: AST → SST)
18	VIR-SST (Statement-oriented Syntax Tree)
19	    ↓ (vir: SST → AIR)
20	AIR (Assertion Intermediate Representation)
21	    ↓ (air: SMT encoding)
22	SMT-LIB queries
23	    ↓ (Z3, and experimentally cvc5)
24	Verification Results
25	```
26	
27	## Crate Architecture
28	
29	### Pipeline Call Graph Overview
30	
31	```
32	main() → Verifier::new() → driver::run()
33	    ↓
34	VerifierCallbacksEraseMacro::after_expansion()
35	    ↓
36	Verifier::construct_vir_crate()
37	    ├─ rustc_hir_analysis::check_crate()  [type check]
38	    └─ rust_to_vir::crate_to_vir()        [HIR → VIR]
39	    ↓
40	Verifier::verify_crate_inner()
41	    ├─ GlobalCtx::new()
42	    ├─ ast_simplify::simplify_krate()
43	    ├─ modes::check_crate()
44	    ├─ buckets::get_buckets()
45	    └─ [per bucket, in parallel]
46	        └─ verify_bucket()
47	            └─ [per function]
48	                ├─ ast_to_sst_func::ast_to_sst_func()
49	                ├─ sst_to_air_func::func_sst_to_air()
50	                └─ Context::query() → SmtProcess::send()
51	```
52

54	### rust_verify
55	
56	The main verifier driver that integrates with `rustc`.  This is the only
57	crate that should interact with `rustc`.  All other crates use Verus-specific
58	constructs.
59	
60	**Key files:**
61	- `main.rs`: Entry point, argument parsing, output formatting
62	- `driver.rs`: Orchestrates `rustc` invocations for verification and compilation
63	- `verifier.rs`: Core `Verifier` struct and verification logic
64	- `context.rs`: `Context<'tcx>` carrying `rustc` state
65	- `config.rs`: Command-line argument definitions (`Args` struct)
66	- `attributes.rs`: Verus attribute parsing (`#[verifier(...)]`)
67	- `lifetime_generate.rs`: Lifetime checking for ghost code.
68	- `trait_*.rs`: Trait conflict checking (see `trait_conflict.rs` for more details)
69	- `rust_to_vir.rs`: Main HIR-to-VIR conversion orchestrator

76	- `Verifier`: Main verifier state including VIR version of the crate(s), statistics, and configuration

80	- `main()`: Entry point

84	- `rust_to_vir::crate_to_vir()`: Converts entire crate to VIR

87	
88	Defines the Verification Intermediate Representation in two forms: AST and SST.
89	The abstract syntax tree (AST) represents the internal subset of Rust that we
90	currently support for verification.  VIR also defines a Statement-oriented
91	Syntax Tree (SST), so that we can convert from Rust's (and VIR's) mutually
92	recursive expression and statement ASTs into a form (the SST) in which
93	expressions do not contain statements.  This simplifies the translation to AIR.
94	
95	**Key files:**
96	- `ast.rs`: VIR-AST definitions (expressions can contain statements)
97	- `sst.rs`: VIR-SST definitions (expressions cannot contain statements)
98	- `context.rs`: `Ctx` and `GlobalCtx` for verification state
99	- `ast_to_sst.rs`, `ast_to_sst_func.rs`: AST→SST conversio

### 🛠️ **Tool result**  ·  22:37:35; tool 11ms

```
1	Verus is an experimental verification framework for Rust-like code.  The main goal is to verify full functional correctness of low-level systems code, building on ideas from existing verification frameworks like [Dafny](https://github.com/dafny-lang/dafny), [Boogie](https://github.com/boogie-org/boogie), [F*](https://github.com/FStarLang/FStar), [VCC](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/project/vcc-a-verifier-for-concurrent-c/), [Prusti](https://github.com/viperproject/prusti-dev), [Cogent](https://github.com/NICTA/cogent), [Coq](https://coq.inria.fr/), and [Isabelle/HOL](https://isabelle.in.tum.de/overview.html).
2	
3	Goals:
4	- provide a pure mathematical language for expressing specifications (like Dafny, F*, Coq, Isabelle/HOL)
5	- provide a mathematical language for expressing proofs (like Dafny, F*, Coq, Isabelle/HOL) based exclusively on classical logic (like Dafny)
6	- provide a low-level, imperative language for expressing executable code (like VCC), based on Rust (like Prusti)
7	- generate small, simple verification conditions that an SMT solver like [Z3](https://github.com/Z3Prover/z3) can solve efficiently, based on the following principles:
8	  - keep the mathematical specification language close to the SMT solver's mathematical language (like Boogie)
9	  - use lightweight linear type checking, rather than SMT solving, to reason about memory and aliasing (like Cogent and [linear Dafny](https://github.com/secure-foundations/dafny/tree/betr/docs/Linear))

13	- ... verify unsafe Rust code (instead, verification will rely on Rust's type safety, as ensured by Rust's type checker)

9	## Some background on ghost variables in Dafny, F*, and Verus
10	
11	For inspiration, I'll look at examples from three verification languages that I'm familiar with:
12	Dafny, F*, and the current version of Verus.
13	(Of course, there are many more languages out there to learn from.)
14	
15	In order to verify executable code,
16	we'll need specifications to say what the executable code is supposed to do,
17	and we'll often need explicit proofs to prove that the executable code meets the specifications.
18	Verus currently uses attributes `#[spec]`, `#[proof]`, and `#[exec]` to mark
19	functions that define specifications, proofs, and executable code:
20	
21	```
22	#[spec]
23	fn is_even(x: u8) -> bool {
24	    x % 2 == 0
25	}
26	
27	#[proof]
28	fn sum_odd_is_even(x: u8, y: u8) {
29	    requires(x as int + (y as int) < 256 && !is_even(x) && !is_even(y));
30	    ensures(is_even(x + y));
31	
32	    // SMT solver proves this automatically
33	}
34	
35	#[exec]
36	fn add_one_and_print(a: u8) {
37	    requires(a < 255 && !is_even(a));
38	
39	    let b = a + 1;
40	    sum_odd_is_even(a, 1);
41	    assert(is_even(b));
42	    print_u8(b);
43	}
44	```
45	
46	The code above would look similar in Dafny,

52	    x % 2 == 0
53	}
54	
55	lemma sum_odd_is_even(x: u8, y: u8)
56	    requires x as int + y as int < 256 && !is_even(x) && !is_even(y)
57	    ensures is_even(x + y)
58	{
59	    // SMT solver proves this automatically
60	}

100	Executable code may contain both specifications and proofs.
101	For example, `add_one_and_print` proves that `a + 1` is even by calling

103	since the SMT solver can figure out that `a + 1` is even without an explicit proof).

107	they do not need to be compiled and they have no runtime representation.

# Three kinds of code ... specification, proof, and executable

As stated in the project [goals](https://github.com/verus-lang/verus/wiki/Goals),
we want to provide a language that expresses specifications, proofs, and executable code.
These three kinds of code differ in significant ways.
For example, executable code is compiled, while proofs and specifications are erased.
In addition, to enable efficient SMT solving,
we [aim](https://github.com/verus-lang/verus/wiki/Goals) to keep the specification language close to the SMT solving language,
whereas executable code and proofs are more similar to programming languages
than to SMT formulas.

We describe these three kinds of code with three different "modes", `spec`, `proof`, and `exec`.
This is a slight extension to the concept of "ghost" and "non-ghost" code
in other verification frameworks like Dafny, in which `exec` corresponds to "non-ghost"
and `spec` and `proof` are two different kinds of "ghost".

Here is an example:
```
#[verifier(opaque)]
#[spec]
fn f(n: int) -> int { n + 1 }

#[proof]
fn lemma_f(n: int) {
    ensures(f(n) > n);

    reveal(f);
}

#[exec]
fn main() {
    #[spec] let x = 7;
    lemma_f(x);
    assert(f(7) > 7);
}
```

or, with a hypothetical future nice syntax:

```
#[verifier(opaque)]
spec fn f(n: int) -> int { n + 1 }

proof fn lemma_f(n: int)
    ensures
        f(n) > n
{
    reveal(f);
}

exec fn main() {
    spec let x = 7;
    lemma_f(x);
    assert(f(7) > 7);
}
```

In this example, `f` is a `spec` function, `lemma_f` is a `proof` function,
`main` is an `exec` function, `n` is a `spec` parameter, `x` is a `spec` variable,
and `f(n) > n` is a `spec` expression.
By default, `exec` function parameters are `exec` and `proof`/`spec` function parameters are `spec`,
so the function declarations above are equivalent to:

```
...
#[spec]
fn f(#[spec] n: int) -> int { n + 1 }

#[proof]
fn lemma_f(#[spec] n: int) {
...
```

There are no `proof` variables or parameters in this example --
we expect `proof` variables to be useful for some special kinds of proof,
but `spec` variables will be more common in standard Hoare-logic style proofs.

## `spec` and `proof` are different

As in Dafny, non-ghost (`exec`) code is compiled,
````

As in Dafny, non-ghost (`exec`) code is compiled,
while ghost (`spec` and `proof`) code is erased before compilation.
However, `spec` and `proof` are treated differently in several ways.
First, `proof` is checked by the Rust lifetime checker,
while `spec` code is not:

```
spec  ---> type checker ---> SMT verifier
proof ---> type checker ---> SMT verifier ---> lifetime checker
exec  ---> type checker ---> SMT verifier ---> lifetime checker ---> compiler
```

Checking proofs for lifetimes enables styles of proof based on linearity,
where a linear `proof` value can represent evidence of the availability of some resource,
as in linear logic and separation logic.
By contrast, `spec` values are free from lifetime constraints:
programs can freely duplicate values within a specification.
More generally, even non-linear `proof` values may be considered evidence that something
has been proven (analogous to how values are used as proofs in constructive logics like Coq),
whereas `spec` values are not by themselves evidence of anything.

Second, proofs may have preconditions and postconditions (requires/ensures),
while specifications do not.
In fact, preconditions and postconditions are the whole point of proofs --
a proof's requires and ensures clause describe what a proof is proving --
but requires and ensures clauses are specifications, not proofs,
and do not carry their own additional requirements or provide
their own additional proofs.
This hard separation between proof and specification is similar to Boogie and Z3,
but differs from Dafny, F*, and Coq, where specifications are themselves verified.
For example, in Dafny, it is an error for a specification like `requires x / y <= 100` to divide by zero,
so that the program has to prove that `y != 0` to even state this specification.
By contrast, Boogie and Z3 treat division by zero in a specification as uninterpreted
rather than errant, and an assertion like `assert(1 / 0 == 1 / 0)` is perfectly valid.

Third, specifications treat all types as inhabited, while proofs (and executable code) do not.
Specifically, for uninhabited types like Rust's `never` type
(written `!` in nightly experimental Rust),
specifications allow for an additional special value called "bottom".
For example, the bottom value can be used to represent results returned by partial functions
that are applied to arguments outside the partial function's domain.
Executable code might create an empty vector `v` of type `vec<!>`.
Subscripting v, as in `v[5]`, would be an error in executable code.
However, specifications can freely refer to `v[5]`,
and the specification expression `v[5]` simply equals bottom.

On the other hand, `spec` and `proof` are similar in one important respect:
both proof functions (lemmas) and specification functions are checked for termination
when they use recursion.
To ensure termination, both `spec` and `proof` functions specify `decreases` clauses
that are checked by the SMT solver.
Proof functions must be checked for termination to avoid circular reasoning --
a proof can't prove itself by simply calling itself recursively infinitely many times.
Specification functions are checked for termination to make sure that they
define meaningful values (a non-terminating function like
`fn f(i: nat) -> nat {f(i) + 1}`
does not actually define a value f(7) such that f(7) = f(7) + 1,
as this is impossible to satisfy.)

## Some language design pitfalls to avoid

The distinction between `spec` and `proof` means that some care must
be taken along the boundary between the two.
In particular, since `spec` includes the bottom value and `proof` does not,
we have to make sure that bottom cannot accidentally flow from `spec` to `proof`
or otherwise malevolently influence proofs.
As described in the section below on mode checking,
it is illegal to directly assign a `spec` value to a `proof` or `exec` variable,
so bottom cannot directly flow into proof variables.
However, there are some more subtle issues.

First, `p

In some situations (e.g. inside a quantifier), we need a pure Exp with Exp::Bind and no Stms instead, so we make a second pass to generate this."

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/ast_to_sst.rs:69-113` - State struct tracks variable renaming via `rename_map` (ScopeMap) and `rename_counters` to eliminate shadowing during SST generation.

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/ast_to_sst.rs:81-92` - Rename strategy: statements extract statements, and variables are renamed using unique integers to avoid collisions; Exp-bound variables can drop numeric IDs when no shadowing occurs.

### 2. Poly/Boxing Type Encoding

**Core Rationale:** SMT solvers don't support polymorphic types; Box/Unbox coercions represent polymorphism with a universal Poly type.

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/poly.rs:1-85` - Comprehensive design rationale:
  - Lines 3-28: "The SMT solver does not support polymorphic types directly, so polymorphism must be encoded by coercing expressions to and from a universal Poly type via Box and Unbox coercions. The predicate has_type describes which underlying type a Box value holds."
  - Lines 12-27: Three competing goals:
    1. Efficiency: use native types where possible (e.g., int, bool) avoiding unnecessary coercions
    2. Efficiency: avoid reasoning about has_type unless necessary
    3. **Completeness**: "avoid adding coercions to variables inside quantifier triggers, because this can cause expressions to fail to match triggers in some cases." Example: `f(g(a))` without coercions fails to match trigger `f(Box(x))`.
  - Lines 38-54: Strategy table distinguishing quantifier variables (always Poly) from exec/proof function parameters (native when monomorphic)
  - Lines 55-68: Quantifiers always use Poly with has_type invariant to avoid trigger mismatch failures
  - Lines 72-85: Exception for arithmetic triggers: use int instead of Poly for arithmetic variables (e.g., `#[trigger] (x * y)`) to match `3 * 4` against triggers involving `Unbox(x)`.

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/poly.rs:106-177` - MonoTyp encoding: only concrete, fully-instantiated types (Bool, Int, specific Datatypes) get native SMT sorts; polymorphic/parametric types map to Poly.

### 3. Mode System Implementation

**Hierarchy:** Exec ≤ Proof ≤ Spec (with mode_le, mode_join, mode_meet operations)

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/modes.rs:21-51` - Mode lattice:
  - Spec is the greatest element (all modes leak into Spec)
  - Exec is the least element
  - Proof is in the middle
  - mode_join computes least upper bound; mode_meet computes greatest lower bound

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/ast.rs:130` - "Ghost (not compiled), used to represent specifications (requires, ensures, invariant)"

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/modes.rs` - Extensive ghost-ness tracking via Proph/ProphVar enums; rejections for non-determinism, mutation captures in closures, etc.

### 4. Recursion &amp; Termination

**Fuel System:** Decreases clauses are encoded via fuel variables (Fuel type, SUCC/ZERO constructors) to control quantifier instantiation.

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/def.rs:47-49` - Fuel naming convention: `"fuel%"` prefix used throughout encoding (FUEL_PARAM, FUEL_TYPE, SUCC, ZERO at lines 133-134, 130-131).

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/recursion.rs:1-116` - Decreases checking:
  - Lines 118-150: `check_decrease()` creates well-formedness constraints: `0 &lt;= decreases_exp &lt; decreases_at_entry` for each decreases clause
  - Fuel used for both recursive functions (loop_id=None) and loops (loop_id=Some)

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/recursive_types.rs:12-47` - Datatype positivity: checks "well-foundedness" ensuring each datatype has at least one base-case variant (no inductive-only cycles). Rationale: "To enable decreases clauses on datatypes while treating the datatypes as inhabited in specs, we need to make sure that the datatypes have base cases, not just inductive cases. This also checks that there is at least one variant, so that spec matches are safe. It also makes sure that (in the formal semantics) we can construct default values for datatypes that aren't just 'bottom', so that the values can be pattern matched (see the OOPSLA 2023 paper and corresponding arXiv paper)."

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/scc.rs` - Tarjan's algorithm (lines 1-6) to compute strongly-connected components for identifying recursive functions and defining fuel variables per SCC.

### 5. Quantifier Triggers

**Manual vs. Automatic Inference Design:**

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/triggers_auto.rs:12-31` - Philosophy: "The goal is to be cautious and avoid triggers that lead to excessive quantifier instantiations, which could lead to SMT timeouts. To that end, the algorithm tries to choose only one trigger for any given quantifier, because multiple triggers lead to more unintended instantiations. The one 'best' trigger is chosen using a rather arbitrary heuristic score. The algorithm selects multiple triggers only if there is a tie for the first-place score between multiple candidates."

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/triggers_auto.rs:136-163` - Heuristic scoring (lower = better):
  - Prefer triggers with fewer terms (e.g., `{f(x, y)}` over `{g(x), h(y)}`)
  - Depth (prefer shallower, next to logical operators not arithmetic)
  - Size (prefer smaller terms)
  - Prefer function calls over constructors/fields
  - Rationale: "REVIEW: these heuristics are experimental -- are they useful in practice? Can they be improved?"

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/triggers.rs:33-42` - Special trigger handling: HeightCompare (internal height function) is user-hidden; triggers rewrite `HeightCompare(...)` to `height(...)` since "it's not useful to trigger on HeightCompare, which is essentially a '&lt;' operator on heights."

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/triggers.rs:47-110` - Native vs. Poly variable classification: quantifier variables used only in arithmetic contexts (Clip, IntegerTypeBound, Arith, Inequality) are marked "native"; otherwise Poly. Rationale: "bound variables are poly by default, so we lean towards poly for vars used both ways; either choice would be ok."

### 6. Special Arithmetic Strategies

**Bitvector Solver Mode:**

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/bitvector_to_air.rs:28-124` - Bitvector specialization: if arch-width is unspecified (Either32Or64), expressions depending on arch-size trigger two queries (32-bit, 64-bit). Rationale: "If the expression depends on the arch size *and* the arch size isn't specified, then we run translation twice, once for 32-bit and once for 64-bit."

**Built-in Symbolic Evaluator (assert_by_compute):**

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/interpreter.rs:1-50` - "A Symbolic Interpreter for VIR... Current target is supporting proof by computation." Memoization of function calls (cache per Fun, indexed by arguments) to handle recursive computations like Fibonacci. Depth limits (DEPTH_LIMIT_MULTIPLIER=500, RLIMIT_MULTIPLIER=400_000) prevent stack overflow and timeout.

### 7. SST to AIR Translation

**Statement Handling, Snapshots, Havoc:**

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/sst_to_air.rs:310-327` - Type ID encoding strategy (decorations separated from types): Decorations (REF, RC, etc.) are kept separate from type IDs to reduce quantifier instantiations. Example: `&amp;Rc&lt;Foo&lt;&amp;bool&gt;&gt;` → decorations (REF (RC $)), types (Foo (REF $) BOOL) instead of nested structure.

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/sst_to_air.rs:522-592` - Type invariants: "If expr has type typ, what can we assume to be true about expr? For refinement types, transparent datatypes potentially containing refinement types, abstract types applied to type variables, and type variables potentially instantiated with refinement types, return Some invariant. For non-refinement types and abstract monotypes, return None."

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/sst_to_air.rs:1601-1656` - Snapshot mechanism for mutation tracking:
  - Snapshot IDs (SNAPSHOT_PRE, SNAPSHOT_CALL, SNAPSHOT_LOOP) track program points
  - Maps used: snapshot_id → SnapPos, span → snapshot ID, span → assigned variables
  - Old expressions reference pre-snapshot values

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/sst_to_air.rs:1750-1760` - Field update encoding: "Semantically equivalent to BinaryOp::FieldUpdate (the SMT update-field), but deliberately mentions each unchanged field explicitly for better quantifier triggering."

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/sst_to_air.rs:2511-2753` - Loop handling:
  - Loop invariants checked at entry and exit
  - Modified variables are havoc'd within the loop (StmtX::Havoc)
  - Snapshots capture state before/after loops
  - Decreases clauses checked via CheckDecreaseHeight

**Loop Invariant Inference:**

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/loop_inference.rs:23-92` - InferSpecForLoopIter for automatic iterator specs: "produces None if any variables in the expression are modified in the loop." Heuristic hints suggest storing iterator in pre-loop variable or using manual invariants.

### 8. Pruning and Reachability

**SMT Context Optimization:**

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/prune.rs:1-123` - Pruning rationale (lines 1-3): "1) Optimize generated SMT by pruning unreachable declarations and definitions. This is strictly an optimization; it should not affect the SMT validity. 2) Also compute names for abstract datatype sorts for the module, since we're traversing the module-visible datatypes anyway."

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/prune.rs:25-43` - ReachedType overapproximation: "For example, if we reach Datatype('D'), and D is generic, we reach D applied to all possible type arguments. (it's ok if we fail to prune away some types)"

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/reachability.rs:1-61` - Graph-based reachability: worklist algorithm computes transitive closure of dependencies from root nodes (exported functions, trait impls, etc.).

### 9. Error Diagnosis and Expansion

**Assertion Expansion:**

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/expand_errors.rs:27-98` - Error expansion via splitting: computes expansion trees to split complex quantifiers and implications, revealing which sub-assertions fail. Used to provide better error messages by showing precisely which introduced hypothesis fails.

### 10. Traits Handling

**Trait Encoding for SMT:**

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/traits.rs:19-150` - Trait resolution: demotes dynamic trait method calls to static calls when concrete impl is available. External trait specs bypass impl resolution; default trait methods use external trait resolution.

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/assoc_types_to_air.rs:1-46` - Associated type projection encoding: generates function `Trait::AssocType(self_type, type_arg_1, ...) → Type_ID`, with axioms linking projections to concrete implementations. Lines 6-10 example: "trait View { type V; } impl View for u8 { type V = u8; } impl&lt;A&gt; View for Vec&lt;u8&gt; { type V = Seq&lt;A&gt; }" → forall axioms declaring View::V(u8) == u8, View::V(Vec A) == Seq(View::V A).

**User-Defined Type Invariants:**

- `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/user_defined_type_invariants.rs:96-129` - Invariants: Datatypes can optionally have a `user_defined_invariant_fn` which is asserted on constructor and assumed on access. - `/var/data/bootstrap/third-party/verus/source/vir/src/heuristics.rs:38-163` - Auto ext_eq heuristic (lines 38-52): "assert and assert-by are sort of tactics for various proof techniques (e.g. nonlinear_arith, bit_vector, compute), and in this spirit, the ordinary assert can supply a default 'tactic' with some basic heuristics. <result># AIR Crate Design Choices Report

## 1. Core AIR Intermediate Representation (ast.rs)

**Type System:**
- TypX enum: Bool, Int, Real, Fun, Named(Ident), BitVec(u32), Float { exp_bits, sig_bits }
  - ast.rs:18-32: Core types support from Int/Bool to IEEE floating point per smt-lib spec (https://smt-lib.org/theories-FloatingPoint.shtml, line 30)
  - Fun type deliberately omits argument/return types to simplify box/unbox for generics (ast.rs:22-23)

**Z3 Special Relations Support:**
- BinaryOp::Relation(Relation, u64) (ast.rs:110-116) encodes Z3's special relations semantics
- Relation enum (ast.rs:85-97): PartialOrder, LinearOrder, TreeOrder, PiecewiseLinearOrder
  - Per Z3 documentation (https://microsoft.github.io/z3guide/docs/theories/Special%20Relations/, ast.rs:83)
  - Each relation gets unique u64 index for solver-level differentiation

**Core Expressions:**
- ExprX::Old(Ident, Ident) (ast.rs:201): reads variable from named snapshot for state capture
- ExprX::Var, ExprX::Const, ExprX::Apply, ExprX::ApplyFun (ast.rs:198-204)
- ExprX::Bind supports Let, Quant (Forall/Exists), Lambda, Choose with triggers and optional qid
  - ast.rs:184-190: Each quantifier/lambda/choose has Triggers, Qid (Option&lt;Ident&gt;) for solver control

**Core Statements (StmtX):**
- Assume(Expr), Assert(AssertId, Message, Filter, Expr) (ast.rs:224-225)
- Havoc(Ident), Assign(Ident, Expr) (ast.rs:226-227)
- Snapshot(Ident) (ast.rs:229): "create a named snapshot of the state of the variables"
- DeadEnd(Stmt) (ast.rs:231): "verify Stmt, but block assumptions in Stmt from persisting after Stmt"
- Breakable/Break for control flow encoding (ast.rs:233-237)
- Block (sequential composition), Switch (nondeterministic choice) (ast.rs:238-240)

**Query Structure:**
- Query = Arc&lt;QueryX&gt; with local declarations and single assertion statement
  - ast.rs:269-272: "checked by SMT with global and local declarations"
